title: Differentiable Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
claim: Smoothing a nonsmooth solution map with a shrinking barrier parameter converges to the exact map, but its derivative stays sharp and discontinuous.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots sharing x-axis, left solution, right derivative, legend in left
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the same horizontal axis, theta, from -2 to 2, and both have grid lines. The left plot shows the solution x* as a function of theta. It is flat at 1 for theta below -1, dips along a parabola to 0 at theta = 0, then rises back to 1 at theta = 1 and stays flat. The right plot shows the derivative of x* with respect to theta. It is zero outside [-1, 1] and a straight line from -2 to 2 inside, with sharp jumps at theta = -1 and theta = 1. A solid black line marks the analytic result. Dashed, dash-dot and dotted colored curves (blue, orange, green, red) mark smoothed approximations with tau = 1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-3 and 1e-2. The curves overlap almost completely. The red dotted curve rounds the corners and jumps visibly, and the derivative plot shows this most. The eye goes first to the kinks and the jumps.
caption: Simple example visualizing a nonsmooth solution map, its derivative and some smooth approximations.
abstract: The efficient computation of parametric solution sensitivities is a key challenge in the integration of learning-enhanced methods with nonlinear model predictive control, as their availability is crucial for many learning algorithms. This paper discusses the computation of solution sensitivities of general nonlinear programs using the implicit function theorem and smoothed optimality conditions treated in interior-point methods (IPM). We introduce sequential barrier quadratic programming (SBQP), which generalizes SQP with an IPM quadratic programming (QP) solver by allowing the barrier parameter to approach a prescribed nonnegative target value, recovering classical SQP when this target is zero. Previous works are limited to convex or unconstrained formulations, or lack an implementation for efficient sensitivity evaluation. The publication is accompanied by an efficient open-source implementation within the `acados` framework, providing both forward and adjoint sensitivities for general optimal control problems, achieving speedups exceeding 3x over the state-of-the-art solvers `mpc.pytorch` and `cvxpygen`.
